name: Tanchangya
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 7 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Debnath, Rupak. 2008. Ethnographic Study of Tanchangya of CHT, CADC, Sittwe and South Tripura. Kolkata: Kreativmind. ISBN 81-88819-31-X. 299 pp. Archive.org item 20230809_20230809_0503.
catalog_locator: ch. 2 'Ethno-linguistics', sec. 2.6 'Language', p. 71; sec. 2.6.2 'Phonology', pp. 74-80, tone paragraph and minimal-pair table p. 79; vowel-length remark p. 74; glottal-stop / low-fall remark p. 76
catalog_quote: [p.71] Tanchangyas speak a distinctly eastern variety of Indo-Aryan, which despite falling in line with the Southeastern (Chittagong) dialect of Bengali, retains several features of Tibeto-Burman, viz., dentalisation of palatal and palato-alveolar obstruents, aspiration of word initial [t], substitution of [r] by [j] in the environment of the palatal vowel [i], and occurrence of tone contrasts with changes in laryngeal and supra-laryngeal settings of phonemes. [p.79] In Tanchangya, there are several pairs of homophonous words, whose precise meanings are conveyed by the speaker using a two-way tonal contrast. On examining a few words (see below), it was found that tone shapes of syllables are affected by changes in voice quality and with elision of consonants. But these findings are only preliminary and require extensive study to arrive at definite conclusions. ... [table, p.79: Tanchangya / Gloss / Tone] za go low level; za jungle low fall; ... asi smile low fall; asi eighty low level; bisi seed low level; bisi mongoose low fall
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.rule_in_words: The only accessible phonological sketch reports a (preliminary) two-way lexical tone contrast, low level vs low fall (e.g. za 'go' vs za 'jungle', bisi 'seed' vs bisi 'mongoose'), and gives no statement on the position or existence of word stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Author states tone shapes are affected by voice quality and consonant elision (glottal stop from IA h- elided leaving a low-fall tone); flags the tonal analysis as preliminary. Vowel length said to be non-distinctive.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level minimal pairs in citation form; sub-dialects by clan (Karwa, Muo, Daingnya, Melong, Mongla, Langbasa, Angya gosa) noted but tone data not localized to one.
new_statements.identity_note: Debnath 2008 describes Tanchangya as spoken in the CHT (Bangladesh), CADC Mizoram and South Tripura (India), with clan-based sub-dialects (Karwa, Muo, Daingnya, Melong, Mongla, Langbasa, Angya gosa); all fall under tang1330 (no Glottolog sub-dialect codes). The closest described sister language is Chakma (chak1266), for which Huziwara 2019 reports a pitch accent system; that must not be transferred to Tanchangya without a source.

tone_statements.citation: Tongchangya World [community author, byline 'Tongchangyaworld']. 2019. In Search History of the Tanchangya Language. Blog essay, Tongchangya World (tongchangyaworld.wordpress.com), posted 1 July 2019, revised 29 June 2021.
tone_statements.quote: Moreover, the Tanchangya language is not tonal. All the syllables in a word and all the words in a sentence receive equal stress like most Indo-Aryan languages. However, most of the Tibeto-Burman languages are tonal languages. Therefore, the subject inherits the verb and the tonal differences clearly show that the Tanchangya language is not a Tibeto-Burman language family but it belongs to the Indo-Aryan European language family.
tone_statements.locator: web page, section 'd. Synthetic Approach', final paragraph before 'e. Stage of Language'

sources.note: A community-scholar essay arguing for Indo-Aryan affiliation; section d ('Synthetic Approach') asserts that Tanchangya is not tonal and that all syllables receive equal stress, using the absence of tone as evidence against a Tibeto-Burman classification. No data or minimal pairs; contradicts Debnath 2008's preliminary low-level vs low-fall contrast (a work listed here) without citing it.
